summary: A report on the second Network Graphics Group meeting at Stanford's AI lab. It covers experiment reports, talks about how graphics connections should work and whether to use one protocol for all display types, and the drafting of a first-pass graphics protocol.

eli5.summary: Notes from a meeting of people working on pictures over the network, about what they tried and what rules to write.

subtitle: Notes from the second Network Graphics Group meeting, where attendees sketched a first-pass graphics protocol.

tldr.problem: People wanted to draw pictures on remote ARPANET computers and displays, but there was no agreed way to connect graphics devices or to describe the pictures.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Graphics Group met at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab, heard reports on experiments and talks, and agreed assumptions and a list of low-level drawing operators for a first-pass output protocol.
tldr.outcome: Committees were set up to draft a Graphics Connection Protocol and the full output protocol. This RFC records the discussion, and its status is listed as Unknown.

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown and it has no recorded replacement. It records the state of the Network Graphics Group's thinking in December 1971, before the committees' drafts existed.

sections.title: The Meeting and Its Agenda
sections.content:
The second Network Graphics Group meeting was held at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab at 6:00 p.m. on Sunday, November 21st. Jim Michener chaired, and M. A. Padlipsky was recording secretary.

The agenda had three topics: reports on experiments set up at the July meeting, prepared talks, and specification of a "first-pass" graphics protocol. Two questions came up early. The first is the context problem: how graphics connections are established and who does what for whom. The second is the console types problem: whether static storage-tube devices and interactive refresh devices need separate protocols. An apparent consensus favoured a single protocol.
sections.eli5: The group got together to decide how drawing on far-away screens should work, and agreed one set of rules would be better than two.

sections.title: Experiment Reports
sections.content:
RAND and UCSB used the UCSB On-Line System from RAND Videographics terminals, and a videotape showed the experiment worked. Larger Host-to-Host allocations gave noticeably smoother drawing, while at minimum allocation the picture appeared a portion at a time because NCP-to-NCP overhead was large.

An SDC and DMCG experiment sending tablet data to a character recognizer was slowed by hardware and software problems and time zone conflicts. An Illinois and Multics experiment was prevented by an NCP bug and a machine switch. A SEX and NIC experiment had not yet been performed. Attendees agreed network host reliability was not crippling to graphics work, but could be quite hampering.
sections.eli5: Some tries worked, like drawing on a far screen. Others were stopped by bugs or by computers being switched off at the wrong time.

sections.title: Connections and Device Types
sections.content:
It was proposed to use the Telnet Protocol for simple graphics, with added control codes for Enter Graphics Mode, Leave Graphics Mode and Console Type. For complex graphics sending an intermediate form, an extra socket pair would be used.

Jim Michener described three kinds of devices: "simple" (ARDS-like), "smart" (IMLAC-like) and "powerful" (E&S-like). He also described three kinds of processing: applications packages, graphics packages, and conversion to device-specific codes. Each can run at the device, the local host or a remote host. A committee of Michener, Bouknight, Harslem and Padlipsky was formed to write a Graphics Connection Protocol, playing a role like the Initial Connection Protocol does for Telnet. The consensus was that only device-specific codes go over Telnet connections unless convincing arguments appear.
sections.eli5: Some screens are simple and some are smart, so the group had to decide who does the thinking: the screen, the nearby computer, or a faraway one.

sections.title: The First-Pass Protocol
sections.content:
The agreed assumptions include a "virtual screen" and a Standard Graphics Stream, with the origin in the center. Coordinates are signed 2's complement fractions from -.5 to +.499, and the stream starts as 8-bit bytes with two-byte coordinates. Text uses Network ASCII. The protocol is organized in levels of complexity: level 0 for simple picture drawing, level 1 for subpicture definition and level 2 for viewport and window operators.

The low-level operators discussed were erase and reset to origin, move, draw, point, line type, line intensity, text and escape. Line types are solid (0), dashed (1) and dotted (2). Intensity runs from 0 (off) through 128 (normal) to 255 (brightest). A protocol committee of Michener, Meyer, Kelly, Cotton and Liddle was to prepare a draft by year's end, with first priority on output rather than input.
sections.eli5: They agreed on a list of simple drawing commands: clear the screen, move the pen, draw a line, put down a dot, write some letters.

viz.caption: LOW-LEVEL OPERATORS DISCUSSED AT THE MEETING

items.label: Erase
items.desc: Erase the screen and reset the beam to the 0,0 center point.

items.label: Move
items.desc: Position the beam without drawing; absolute, relative and local modes.

items.label: Draw
items.desc: Draw a line of the current type to the given x, y position.

items.label: Point
items.desc: Display a point at the specified position.

items.label: Line type
items.desc: Solid (0), dashed (1) or dotted (2) until further notice.

items.label: Line intensity
items.desc: 0 is off, 128 is normal, 255 is brightest.

items.label: Text
items.desc: Display a number of Network ASCII characters.

items.label: Escape
items.desc: Pass a number of bytes directly to a console of a given type.
